newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC eyes a quota freeze for Iraq's return.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC eyes a quota freeze for Iraq's return.

text.p: A consensus was emerging at OPEC talks on Wednesday on freezing cartel output quotas to try to buoy high oil prices now that the United Nations seems set to relax its Gulf War ban on sales by Iraq.

Ministers said the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries needed to exercise caution in setting 1997 production levels because of doubts on how winter weather may affect fuel demand and about the impact of an Iraqi return to the market.
Iraq's chief delegate, Osama al-Hiti, told reporters he expected Baghdad would resume oil sales in "a matter of weeks".
A Security Council sanctions committee approved a pricing formula for its food-for-oil deal with Iraq on Wednesday , removing one of the final hurdles.
"If the tanker comes tomorrow we can fill it up", al-Hiti said. Baghdad, which hosted the 1960 founding meeting of OPEC, hasn't been allowed to sell oil since it invaded fellow member Kuwait in 1990.
Delegates at the OPEC talks in Vienna said cartel linchpin Saudi Arabia favours a freeze at least to the end of June on current quotas, which already include provision for Iraq.

Ministers who told reporters they also favour a "rollover" included Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh. He said he would support a 12-month freeze, although Algeria's Amar Makhloufi said he thought that the consensus was for six months.
A brief plenary session of the 101st OPEC ministerial meeting adjourned to 0900 GMT on Thursday when substantive discussion of quotas will begin. Ministers say talks may end on Thursday.
Iraq's deal with the U.N. would let it sell $2 billion worth of oil to help buy food and medicine.
Al-Hiti says only "very minor technicalities" now need to be ironed out. He expected to export 700,000 to 800,000 barrels daily using up in full his OPEC quota allocation.

Iran's Aqazadeh meanwhile aired the vexed matter of quota violations at talks with Erwin Arrieta of Venezuela, alleged to be most in excess, but said later that Arrieta "did not accept even one barrel of over-production".
Traders say OPEC would be best advised to sidestep thorny issues and avoid public haggling that might alarm a skittish futures market and jeopardise a surprise 1996 rally in prices.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude is trading now around $23 a barrel compared with only $18 back in June when OPEC last met, mainly because of a rush to fill depleted Western stocks of heating fuel ahead of what may be a harsh northern winter.

"OPEC is meeting against a backdrop that can only bring a smile to their lips", said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at brokers Smith Barney. "Oil is up five dollars. That is in itself an incentive to preserve the status quo".
Prices are strong despite both the prospect that the ban on Iraqi exports will be relaxed and OPEC's own quota violations.

Alleged excess is said by Western monitors to have already propelled OPEC volume a million barrels daily above a ceiling agreed at 25.03 million, even before 800,000 extra that has been pencilled in for Iraq begins to flow.
But delegates say Saudi Arabia feels the market can absorb more oil, because stocks are low and as a result of the delay so far on resumed Iraqi sales.
The weather is another imponderable for world oil prices.
Depending on its severity, the northern winter can swing petroleum demand by a million barrels daily, Barclays Bank economists note in their latest Commodities Survey.
They have raised their forecast for average 1996 prices to $20 per barrel from only $16.8 in 1995. But they add that "our view remains that prices are likely to ease next year".
Their view that they'll ease by maybe $1 is based on the "strong possibility" of revived Iraqi exports and a prospect of more supply from the North Sea, Asia and Latin America.
